validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE/CLASSIFICATION/DUPLICATE all confirmed at high confidence — this is an unusually well-documented small connector line for a state-jurisdictional (not FERC) project. This is an INTRASTATE Michigan project so FERC silence is expected and is not an existence concern (SOP point (b)); the correct venue is the Michigan Public Service Commission, and I found it: SEMCO Energy Gas Co. filed for Act 9 (Public Act 9 of 1929) siting approval in December 2016 and the MPSC approved a settlement allowing construction under Case No. U-18202 in August 2017, per the MPSC's own Oct. 25, 2017 press release (mi-psc.my.site.com/.../068t0000001UW23AAG: 'In August, the MPSC approved a settlement agreement to improve natural gas reliability by allowing SEMCO to build the nearly 43-mile Marquette Connector natural gas pipeline (Case No. U-18202)'). A second, entirely independent MPSC document — a March 2025 cross-examination transcript from a LATER, unrelated SEMCO docket (Case No. U-21780, SEMCO's application for the Keweenaw Connector Pipeline) — references the Marquette Connector Pipeline (MCP) as existing background infrastructure and states its capacity in sworn testimony, which is strong proof this is a real, still-operating asset years after completion, not a GEM-only entity. Independent secondary corroboration beyond the two MPSC documents: Burns & McDonnell's contractor case-study page (engineering/construction-management contractor on the project); SEMCO's own Feb-2017 planning presentation hosted on marquette.org (the Marquette County/chamber site); Pipeline & Gas Journal's Oct-2018 'Planned Pipelines' industry listing (independent trade press); three separate Mining Journal (local newspaper) articles from March 2017, May 2019 and November 2019; and a WLUC-TV (Upper Michigan's Source) news article from September 2019. That is at least five distinct independent origins (state regulator, contractor, trade press, newspaper, TV news) all describing the same 42-mile, 10-/20-inch SEMCO Energy connector between the Northern Natural Gas and Great Lakes Gas Transmission systems in Marquette County, MI, completed/operational in November-December 2019. CLASSIFICATION correct: this is a large-diameter (10in/20in) interstate-system INTERCONNECTOR built to FERC-jurisdictional-grade specs even though it is itself state-regulated — correctly a transmission line, not a gathering/distribution main (SEMCO's own distribution mains in Michigan run to 6,000 miles per the marquette.org presentation and are a separate system). DUPLICATE check against the 46-row roster: no other row describes this route (Arnold/Wells Township – Negaunee Township – Marquette, Marquette County, MI); it is not the same pipe as any of the other Michigan rows (P0225 NEXUS, P0375 Saginaw Trail, the four Rover rows, P2505/P3202 Vector, P0288/P2531 Empire) — all of those are in different counties/corridors. LOCATION: GEM's StartLocation=Arnold / EndLocation=Negaunee, both StartState/Province and EndState/Province=Michigan, are all independently confirmed — Pipeline & Gas Journal's listing states 'Location: Arnold, MI - Negaunee Township, MI' verbatim, and both the March-2017 and November-2019 Mining Journal articles independently describe the same two termini ('connect the Great Lakes Gas Transmission system near Arnold ... with Northern Natural Gas' system to the north in Marquette' / 'runs from Negaunee Township to Arnold'). LENGTH=42.00 mi and DIAMETER='10, 20' in are each confirmed by at least three independent sources: Pipeline & Gas Journal states 'Length: 42 miles / Diameter: 10 and 20 inches' exactly; the March-2017 and November-2019 Mining Journal articles both break it down as a 36.2-/36-mile 20-inch main line plus a 6.4-/6-mile 10-inch lateral (summing to 42.6-42.7 mi, which every source nonetheless headlines as '42-' or 'nearly 43-mile' — treated as consistent with GEM's 42.00, not a material discrepancy); the marquette.org presentation and Burns & McDonnell page independently confirm the 10in/20in two-segment design. STARTYEAR1=2019 is confirmed by the Nov-2019 Mining Journal article ('gassing up that pipeline late in the month, just right after Thanksgiving'), the Sept-2019 WLUC-TV article ('SEMCO hopes the pipeline will be online in November'), and Burns & McDonnell's project-stats box ('Completion Date December 2019') — all pointing to the same late-Nov/early-Dec 2019 in-service window. CAPACITY=144 MMcf/d is confirmed independently by Burns & McDonnell ('144M CUBIC FEET OF NATURAL GAS DELIVERED PER DAY') and, separately, by SEMCO's own sworn testimony in the unrelated 2025 MPSC Keweenaw Connector docket ('the MCP's capacity of approximately 6,000 Mcf/hr (or 144,000 Mcf/day)') — two independent origins, high tier. OWNER/OPERATOR: SEMCO Energy Gas Co. (a subsidiary of AltaGas per Burns & McDonnell) is confirmed as sole owner/builder/operator by every source read; GEM's Owner1='SEMCO Energy' 100% is correct. Opened and read to exhaustion all 5 harvested wiki citations for this row (Pipeline News PDF, Burns & McDonnell case study, marquette.org presentation, Mining Journal Nov-2019 article, marquetteconnectorfacts.com) plus 5 additional sources found via targeted search per the sweep's source ladder (2 MPSC documents, 2 more Mining Journal articles, 1 WLUC-TV article) — 10 sources total opened. marquetteconnectorfacts.com (the harvested SEMCO facts-site citation) failed to resolve (ConnectionError — the microsite appears to be down/retired); not cited, no working Wayback snapshot located in the time available, flagging rather than silently dropping it.

validity.recommendation: update SegmentCost from the $137.5M pre-construction estimate to the ~$159M actual final cost SEMCO reported once the project was complete (or, at minimum, pair the current value with a SegmentCostYear/note marking it as a pre-construction estimate rather than the actual cost)
validity.researcher_notes: GEM records SegmentCost=137,500,000 USD with no ref. That figure is exactly the midpoint of a PRE-CONSTRUCTION ESTIMATE, not the project's actual final cost. Two independent sources give the same pre-construction estimate that GEM's number traces to: SEMCO's own Feb-2017 planning presentation ('Total Cost: Approximately $135-$140 Million') and, independently, the Mining Journal's March-2017 article on the project's environmental filing ('the roughly $135 million project'). But a THIRD, later and more authoritative source — the Mining Journal's November-2019 article, published as construction was wrapping up, quoting SEMCO spokesman Tim Lubbers directly — states a materially different, higher actual cost: 'The total final cost of the project is estimated to be around $159 million, Lubbers said.' $159M vs. GEM's $137.5M is a ~15.6% increase, consistent with the kind of cost overrun disclosed for other pipelines in this same batch (e.g. Mountaineer XPress) and plausible given the wetland-crossing, rock-excavation, and delayed-fencing/grading complications documented in the Burns & McDonnell case study and the same Nov-2019 article. I could not find a second, independent source stating the $159M actual-cost figure in so many words — it comes from one company spokesman quote reported by one outlet — so I am flagging this as a contested value rather than silently overwriting the cell, at medium-tier support for the $159M candidate specifically (the $137.5M value, by contrast, is well corroborated as an ESTIMATE, just not as the ACTUAL cost). Searched Pipeline & Gas Journal's planned-projects listing, the two MPSC documents, and the WLUC-TV article for a second actual-cost figure; none give one.
